semantics.note: The normalisation keeps the two-year comparison and both uses of 'many'. It is a perception observation, but a vague one with no population or measure.

contract.note: The contract fairly finds no testable reading. 'Many' is undefined and 'oracle' and 'snake oil salesman' are metaphors, so the claim cannot be scored.

evidence.note: A CNBC report from August 2025 in which an academic uses 'snake oil' about AI firms in general, not Altman. It cannot measure what 'many' people thought.

reviews.rationale: The claim is about how 'many' people saw Altman, with no defined population, measure or threshold, and it uses metaphorical labels. No polling or systematic measure exists. It is untestable, so not_adjudicable.

semantics.note: The unhedged 'will' makes this a forecast with no deadline. 'Self-correcting' is a general premise, kept verbatim.

contract.note: In context, 'from the ashes' refers to the faltering of LLM scaling, so reading it as alternatives rising after that paradigm fails is fair. The contract also correctly says absence of the event cannot count as failure while there is no deadline.

evidence.note: LeCun's AMI raised about $1B for world models in March 2026, but alongside a still-dominant LLM industry. This is not displacement of LLMs, so it meets neither early-resolution rule.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. Neither early-resolution condition was met by the evaluation date: LLM scaling was not displaced, and no LLM system was accepted as AGI. Well-funded alternatives exist but do not settle it. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Two firm observations about the GPT-5 launch week, faithfully rendered.

contract.note: 'Almost nobody' is unscoped, so the plain reading (satisfaction was rare across users, including business customers) is ordinary and fair. Part A's test is also fair.

evidence.note: A TechRepublic report from August 2025: users demanded GPT-4o back and OpenAI reinstated it. This supports Part A.
A CNBC report from August 14: Cursor, Vercel and Factory made GPT-5 their default within a week. That shows substantial satisfied business users.
The same CNBC article: Box's CEO praised GPT-5 strongly in the launch week.
The Decoder, August 9: users were 'split' and some preferred GPT-4o. This confirms Part A and leans against near-universal dissatisfaction.

reviews.rationale: Part A holds: users demanded GPT-4o back and OpenAI restored it. Part B ('almost nobody felt satisfied') is contradicted: launch-week reports show several enterprise and developer customers adopting and praising GPT-5, and users split rather than nearly all dissatisfied.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Broadly faithful, though it narrows 'three years of hype' to GPT-5 promises and drops the 'primary mission' aside, which the contract nonetheless tests.

contract.note: Full support requires documentary proof that GPT-5 was Altman's 'primary mission', a rhetorical aside the normalised claim omits. That stretches the test against the speaker. The AGI and shortfall tests are otherwise reasonable.

evidence.note: Altman's February 2025 roadmap promises a unified GPT-5 system, not AGI. Nothing in the packet shows this promise was missed.
Business Insider, August 7, 2025: Altman himself said GPT-5 falls short of AGI, missing continuous learning. This supports the non-AGI clause.
OpenAI's own launch disclosure claims gains and expert-level results in about half of knowledge-work cases. It is company self-reporting and neither shows AGI nor settles which promises were met.

reviews.rationale: The non-AGI clause is supported, since Altman conceded GPT-5 is not AGI. The packet does not show which documented promises GPT-5 materially missed, and it has no evidence on the 'primary mission' clause. Nothing contradicts any part, but the full claim is not settled.
